items.stem: What is the money supply?
options: The total amount of money (cash and bank deposits) in the economy
The total value of goods produced
The amount of cash held by the central bank only
items.answer: The total amount of money (cash and bank deposits) in the economy
items.markingKey: Narrow and broad measures.

items.stem: Explain two functions of a central bank.
items.answer: Conducts monetary policy (interest rates, money supply); issues notes and coins; banker to the government; banker to commercial banks/lender of last resort; supervises the financial system; manages reserves and exchange rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each function explained [2]

items.stem: Explain how commercial banks can increase the money supply.
items.answer: When banks make loans they create deposits in borrowers’ accounts, which can be spent and re-deposited; bank lending therefore increases broad money.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loans create deposits; 1 mark: increases money supply [2]

items.stem: The central bank of Lunaria sets its policy interest rate at 4%. Inflation is 1%. Calculate the approximate real interest rate.

The central bank of Selmaria sets its policy interest rate at 6%. Inflation is 3%. (a) Calculate the real interest rate. (b) Explain how the real interest rate affects the incentive to borrow and to save. (c) Explain whether monetary policy is tight or loose.
items.answer: (a) +3% (b) A higher real rate raises the real cost of borrowing and reward for saving, reducing spending; a negative real rate encourages borrowing and discourages saving. (c) Tight: positive real rate restrains AD.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) borrowing and saving effects [2] (c) [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Inflation in Lunaria reached 9%, well above the central bank’s 2% target. Over 18 months the central bank raised its policy rate from 0.5% to 4% and stopped its programme of quantitative easing. House prices began to fall and the currency appreciated. Business groups warned that higher rates would push the economy into recession. (a) Calculate the real policy interest rate at the end of the period, assuming inflation is still 9%. (b) Explain why falling house prices might reduce consumption.
items.answer: (a) −5% (b) Negative wealth effect; less equity to borrow against; confidence falls.
items.markingKey: (a) 4 − 9 [1] (b) Credit: Negative wealth effect; less equity to borrow against; confidence falls. [2]

items.stem: What is the interest rate?
options: The price of borrowing money and the reward for saving
items.answer: The price of borrowing money and the reward for saving
items.markingKey: Cost of credit.

items.stem: The central bank of Fendaria is given independence to set interest rates. Explain why this might lead to lower inflation.
items.answer: Independent central banks can make unpopular decisions (raising rates) without political pressure; this makes inflation targets credible, lowering inflation expectations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no political pressure; 1 mark: credibility/expectations [2]

items.stem: The central bank of Fendaria sets its policy interest rate at 6%. Inflation is 9%. Calculate the approximate real interest rate.

The central bank of Umbria Nova sets its policy interest rate at 4%. Inflation is 2%. (a) Calculate the real interest rate. (b) Explain how the real interest rate affects the incentive to borrow and to save. (c) Explain whether monetary policy is tight or loose.
items.answer: (a) +2% (b) A higher real rate raises the real cost of borrowing and reward for saving, reducing spending; a negative real rate encourages borrowing and discourages saving. (c) Tight: positive real rate restrains AD.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) borrowing and saving effects [2] (c) [1] [4]

items.stem: A policy institute in Doha has published a report on this issue for the government of Ostrelia. Explain the functions of a central bank.
items.answer: Monetary policy, issuing currency, banker to government and banks, lender of last resort, financial regulation, managing reserves.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Monetary policy, issuing currency, banker to government and banks, lender of last resort, financial regulation, managing reserves. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: What is quantitative easing?
options: The central bank buying financial assets to increase the money supply
The government printing money to pay wages
items.answer: The central bank buying financial assets to increase the money supply
items.markingKey: Asset purchases with new central bank money.

items.stem: Explain how quantitative easing is intended to increase aggregate demand.
items.answer: The central bank buys bonds, raising their prices and lowering long-term interest rates; banks gain reserves to lend; cheaper credit and higher asset prices raise consumption and investment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: asset purchases; 1 mark: lower long-term rates/more lending; 1 mark: C and I rise [3]

items.stem: Interest rates in Valdoria are already 0.1% and the economy is in recession. Explain why the central bank might use quantitative easing.
items.answer: It cannot cut rates further, so it buys assets to increase the money supply and reduce long-term rates, encouraging spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: zero lower bound; 1 mark: QE mechanism [2]

items.stem: The central bank of Rovania buys $50bn of government bonds from banks. Is this expansionary or contractionary monetary policy?
items.answer: Expansionary monetary policy
items.markingKey: Expansionary monetary policy: quantitative easing increases the money supply and lowers long-term interest rates.

items.stem: The central bank of Nordavia raises interest rates to curb inflation. Is this expansionary or contractionary monetary policy? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Contractionary monetary policy: dearer borrowing reduces spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Contractionary monetary policy; 1 mark: explanation – dearer borrowing reduces spending. [2]

items.stem: Classify each measure and explain how it works. (i) The central bank of Pelora raises interest rates to curb inflation. (ii) The central bank of Pelora buys $50bn of government bonds from banks.
items.answer: (i) Contractionary monetary policy (ii) Expansionary monetary policy
items.markingKey: (i) Contractionary monetary policy – dearer borrowing reduces spending. [2] (ii) Expansionary monetary policy – quantitative easing increases the money supply and lowers long-term interest rates. [2] Total [4]

items.answer: (a) −5.5% (b) Negative wealth effect; less equity to borrow against; confidence falls.
items.markingKey: (a) 3.5 − 9 [1] (b) Credit: Negative wealth effect; less equity to borrow against; confidence falls. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Inflation in Valdoria reached 7%, well above the central bank’s 2% target. items.stem: Arjun, an economics student in Toronto, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. Discuss whether quantitative easing is an effective policy when interest rates are close to zero.
items.answer: For: Lowers long-term rates, supports asset prices and lending, prevents deflation. Against: Banks may not lend; benefits asset holders (inequality); inflation risk later; diminishing effect; judgement. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Lowers long-term rates, supports asset prices and lending, prevents deflation. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Banks may not lend; benefits asset holders (inequality); inflation risk later; diminishing effect; judgement. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: How does a cut in interest rates increase consumption?
options: It raises the price of imports
It reduces the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving
items.answer: It reduces the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving
items.markingKey: Credit cheaper; mortgage payments fall.

items.stem: Explain how a rise in interest rates reduces inflation.
items.answer: Borrowing becomes dearer and saving more attractive, so consumption and investment fall; mortgage costs rise; the currency may appreciate, reducing net exports and import prices; AD falls, reducing demand-pull inflation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each channel (max 3) [3]

items.stem: Explain one reason why monetary policy may take time to affect inflation.
items.answer: Loans and mortgages may be on fixed rates; firms’ investment plans take time to change; prices adjust slowly; lags of 18–24 months.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reason; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: Arjun has an interest-only mortgage of $150,000. The interest rate changes from 5% to 4% after a central bank decision. Calculate the change in annual interest payments.

Sofia has an interest-only mortgage of $200,000. The interest rate changes from 4% to 5.5% after a central bank decision. (a) Calculate the annual interest payments before and after. (b) Explain how this change, repeated across many households, affects aggregate demand and inflation.
items.answer: (a) $8,000 → $11,000 (b) Higher payments reduce disposable income and consumption; AD falls, reducing inflationary pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) both [2] (b) disposable income → C → AD [1]; inflation [1] [4]
